questions.stem: In the reaction CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂, what is the atom economy for producing calcium oxide? [Mr: CaCO₃ = 100, CaO = 56, CO₂ = 44]
questions.explanation: Atom economy = (Mr of desired product / total Mr of all products) x 100 = (56 / (56 + 44)) x 100 = (56/100) x 100 = 56%. This means 56% of the mass of reactants ends up as the desired product, and 44% becomes waste (CO₂). Note: we use the sum of Mr of ALL products in the denominator.

questions.stem: Why is a high atom economy desirable in industrial chemistry?

options.text: It means the reaction happens faster
It reduces waste, which is better for the environment and more cost-effective
It increases the melting point of the product
It means fewer reactants are needed

questions.explanation: A high atom economy means a larger proportion of the atoms in the reactants end up in the desired product, with less waste. This is important because less waste means lower disposal costs, less environmental impact, and better use of raw materials. This is a key principle of green chemistry and sustainable chemical manufacturing.

questions.stem: Which type of reaction always has 100% atom economy?

options.text: Addition reactions (where all atoms end up in one product)

questions.explanation: Addition reactions have 100% atom economy because all the atoms from the reactants end up in a single product with no by-products. For example: CH₂=CH₂ + H₂ → CH₃CH₃. All atoms from the reactants are in the product. Decomposition, neutralisation, and combustion all produce multiple products, so their atom economy for any single product is less than 100%.

questions.stem: Hydrogen can be made by two methods: (1) CH₄ + H₂O → CO + 3H₂ or (2) 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂. Which has the higher atom economy for hydrogen production? [Mr: H₂ = 2, CO = 28, O₂ = 32, CH₄ = 16, H₂O = 18]

options.text: Both have the same atom economy

questions.explanation: Method 1: Atom economy = (3 x 2)/(28 + 3 x 2) x 100 = 6/34 x 100 = 17.6%. Method 2: Atom economy = (2 x 2)/(2 x 2 + 32) x 100 = 4/36 x 100 = 11.1%. Method 1 has a higher atom economy for H₂ production. However, note the CO by-product in method 1 might itself be useful in other processes.

questions.stem: How does atom economy differ from percentage yield?

options.text: Atom economy is about the theoretical efficiency of the reaction equation; percentage yield is about how much product is actually obtained in practice
Percentage yield is always higher than atom economy
Atom economy considers the mass of reactants; percentage yield does not

questions.explanation: Atom economy is calculated from the balanced equation and measures what proportion of reactant atoms could theoretically become the desired product - it is a property of the reaction itself. Percentage yield measures how much product was actually obtained compared to the theoretical maximum - it depends on practical factors like losses and incomplete reactions. A reaction can have 100% atom economy but less than 100% yield.
